title: Colleagues
hook: the Sigalovada's duties between workers and employers (DN 31)
tomorrow: how do you stop carrying work home every night?

segments.voice: Yesterday: speech at work. Kind at work, true and in a voice someone can take in. Today, the people on the other end of those messages.
screen: `KIND AT WORK.` → `THE PEOPLE ON THE OTHER END.`

segments.voice: Some workplaces call themselves a family, and some bosses act as if that means you owe them your weekends. The Sigalovada Sutta has a clearer answer. A young man named Sigala bows to the six directions every morning, because his father told him to. The Buddha meets him and gives the old ritual a new meaning: each direction is a relationship. Parents, teachers, family, friends, spiritual guides. And below, the Buddha says, are workers and servants. So what does a boss owe you, and what do you owe back? The sutta's answer is a list, and it runs both ways.
screen: `WE'RE A FAMILY HERE.` → `SIGALA BOWS TO SIX DIRECTIONS.` → `EACH DIRECTION, A RELATIONSHIP.` → `IT RUNS BOTH WAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the list. An employer looks after workers in five ways: work suited to their strength; food and wages; care when they're sick; a share of special treats; and time off at the right times. And workers, looked after like that, give back: they start before the employer and finish after, take only what's given, do their work well, and speak well of the employer. Notice the shape. Not a ladder where care only flows up. A loop. Work matched to strength sounds a lot like not burning people out. Time off at the right times sounds a lot like a weekend. And doing the work well and speaking well of the place: that's what a good colleague returns. Be honest about the setting, too. This is an ancient household with servants, and some lines, like starting before the master, belong to that world. What carries over is the loop. Each side has duties, and each side's care makes the other's easier. Colleagues, in the sutta's sense, aren't a family, and they aren't strangers. They're people bound by duties both ways.
screen: `THE EMPLOYER'S FIVE DUTIES.` · `WHAT WORKERS GIVE BACK.` · `NOT A LADDER. A LOOP.` · `AN ANCIENT HOUSEHOLD, HONESTLY.` · then, large: `DUTIES BOTH WAYS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you work or study alongside. Pick one duty from the list that fits: take a task that suits your strength, share something good, or speak well of them somewhere they'll never hear it. Choose when you'll do it, and see yourself doing it.
Colleagues: people bound by duties both ways, care from those in charge, and good work and good words returned.
Keep this one: duties both ways, a loop and not a ladder. Five of fifty.

howItsDone: The Sigalovada Sutta is taught in Theravada communities as a code of conduct for lay people, and its duties between employers and workers are read as guidance for workplaces today.

fork.setup: your manager covered your shift when you were sick. now a coworker is trashing her in the break room. what fits duties both ways?
options: speak well of her, honestly; that's part of what workers give back.
join in; complaining together is how coworkers bond.
stay out of it; duties at work are only about the tasks.
fork.reveal: in the sutta, workers return care by doing good work and speaking well of the employer. a loop, not a ladder.

original.note: Pali: kammakara, a worker; DN 31 places servants and workers in the lower direction.

what a scholar hears: DN 31, the Sigalovada Sutta, maps servants and workers to the nadir and lists five duties on each side, in an ancient household setting.

chat.says: petrov said fine, call them solid pine. AND he gave me finals weekend off. i feel like i owe him?
options: Not a debt. Duties run both ways: he gave time off; you do good work, speak well.
You owe him extra shifts now. Every favor from a boss has to be paid back.
Nothing. Time off is his job, and workers don't owe a boss anything back.
chat.meaning: In the Sigalovada Sutta, employers owe fair work, wages, care and time off; workers return good work and good words. A loop, not a debt.

tie.story: The Buddha told Sigala that employers and workers each owe the other: fair work and time off one way, good work and good words the other.
tie.friend: Mai doesn't owe Mr. Petrov a favor; she can return his care with careful work and honest words about the shop.
tie.you: who's one person at work or school you could do a small duty for?

notes: Life shape: a week's situation (a boss who gave time off; does Mai owe him?) and what the tradition gives for it; the chat leads.

DN 31 paraphrased: the master ministers to servants and workers by assigning work according to strength, supplying food and wages, tending them in sickness, sharing delicacies, and granting leave at times; they rise before him, lie down after him, take only what is given, do their work well, and carry about his praise. Rhys Davids' 1921 translation (Dialogues III) exists but was not quoted. Confirm wording.

Sigala bows to the directions because his father told him to (the sutta: his father's dying instruction); the lesson leaves out 'dying'. The directions list in the hook (parents, teachers, family, friends, spiritual guides, and workers below) is condensed; confirm.
The lesson names the household setting (servants, 'starting before the master') honestly as ancient; confirm the framing.
